newsitem.title: USA: Spy case will not damage U.S.-Seoul ties - Perry.
newsitem.headline: Spy case will not damage U.S.-Seoul ties - Perry.

text.p: The arrest of a U.S. Navy intelligence employee on charges of spying for South Korea will not damage close military ties between the two countries, U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Sunday.

"We have a compelling reason for maintaining a strong military alliance with South Korea. We are both profoundly affected by the threat from North Korea. That threat still is very much on our minds," he told reporters flying home with him from a visit to Nordic countries.

Perry refused for legal reasons to comment directly on the arrest in Washington on Tuesday of Robert Kim, 56, an 18-year government employee who worked at a U.S. Navy intelligence office in Suitland, Maryland. But asked if the incident would hurt Washington and Seoul's four-decade-old ties, he said without hesitation:

"To directly answer your question, both the Republic of South Korea and the United States believe that the military alliance between our two countries is of vital importance to our countries, and we will maintain and, if anything, strengthen that military alliance."

Kim, arrested at a diplomatic reception at Fort Myer, Virginia, was charged with passing classified information to a South Korean agent, a naval attache at the embassy in Washington identified as Capt. Dong-Il Baek.
"I'll just say I'm not easily surprised," Perry said when asked if the incident surprised him. "I've been around too long to be surprised by almost anything anymore."

Perry suggested that the Kim incident was far outweighed by mutual worries about North Korea. He mentioned the recent grounding of a North Korean submarine off South Korea and the subsequent killing of a number of men from that submarine by the South Korean military.

"Everything that has happened in the last month or two only reinforces our view that the alliance with Korea is very important, and we will sustain it -- both the pluses and the minuses that have happened -- we are still going to go ahead and sustain that alliance," he said before landing at nearby Andrews Air Force Base.
His comments reinforced earlier statements by the White House to the effect that ties with South Korea were too important to be seriously damaged by the actions of an individual.
Kim, of Sterling, Virginia, was born in Seoul and became a U.S. citizen in 1974. He was charged with passing the classified information from May through September.

Kim has been held in jail under an espionage law that carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison. He faces a hearing before a federal magistrate on Monday on whether he should continue to be held without bail.
Perry earlier urged both South and North Korea to use restraint and limit the damage from the submarine incident earlier this month.

The United States maintains 37,000 troops in South Korea as a deterrent against any attack from the North. It is anxious to prevent the incident from endangering a proposal Washington and Seoul have put to Pyongyang for four-way peace talks, also including China.

Perry returned to Washington on Sunday from a nine-day trip to Scandanavia that included two days of talks in Bergen, Norway, with NATO defence ministers and Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov on Bosnia and on Western relations with Moscow.
